passages.happening:
Five sisters come forward: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, the daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh. They come to the entrance of the tent and stand ‘before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders, and the whole congregation’ (verse 2).

They say, “Our father died in the wilderness, but he was not among the followers of Korah who gathered together against the LORD. Instead, he died because of his own sin, and he had no sons. Why should the name of our father disappear from his clan because he had no sons? Give us property among our father’s brothers” (verses 3-4).

“So Moses brought their case before the LORD” (verse 5).

God answers, “The daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly. You certainly must give them property as an inheritance among their father’s brothers, and transfer their father’s inheritance to them” (verse 7). Then he makes it a law for all Israel: “If a man dies and leaves no son, you are to transfer his inheritance to his daughter” (verse 8). If there is no daughter, it goes to his brothers, then to his father's brothers, then to the nearest relative in the clan (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
The census of chapter 26 counted the heirs of the land, and it paused over one man who had only daughters. Now those daughters step forward, and the book gives them the floor.

In Israel, as in most of the ancient world, land passed from father to son. The census had listed men. When the land was divided, a man with no sons would have no one to receive a share. His land would be taken into the holdings of his relatives. His name would drop out of the clan's memory, and his daughters would have nothing of their own.

Notice what the sisters do. They do not wait for someone to speak for them. They go to the most public place in the camp, the entrance of the tent, where cases were judged. They stand before Moses, the high priest, the leaders and the whole assembly. Five unmarried women address the entire leadership of the nation about a matter of law. That took courage.

Their argument is careful. First they clear their father's name. He was not one of Korah's rebels, whose share might have been thought forfeit. He died as the rest of his generation died. Then they ask their question: why should a man's name disappear because he had no sons? Then they make their request, plainly: give us land.

They are also asking in faith. Not a field of Canaan had yet been taken. Their fathers had refused the land. These five are claiming a share in it before the Jordan is crossed. They believe the promise more firmly than the generation that died.

Moses does not rule on it himself, and he does not send them away. This is one of the cases in the book where the law has not yet spoken, and Moses takes it to God.

God's answer begins with his verdict on the women: they ‘speak correctly’. They are right. He does not grant a favor to five persistent sisters. He says that what they asked is just. Then he widens their case into a standing law, with an order of inheritance that moves outward from son to daughter to brothers to uncles to the nearest relative.

Five women challenged a custom, and God's law for the whole nation was changed at their word. The Bible names all five every time it tells the story: in the census, here, in chapter 36, and again in Joshua.

Legal texts from Mesopotamia show that daughters could sometimes inherit when there were no sons, though customs varied. Several of the sisters' names are also known as place names in the hill country of Manasseh. Tirzah later became a royal city of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 15:33). The clans descended from these women left their mark on the land.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua records that the ruling was kept. The sisters came to Eleazar and Joshua and said, “The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.” And ‘Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father’s brothers’ (Joshua 17:4).

Job, at the end of his story, did for his daughters what this law required only when there were no sons: ‘their father granted them an inheritance among their brothers’ (Job 42:15).

Paul uses the language of inheritance for all who belong to Christ, with no distinction: ‘neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus’, and all are ‘heirs according to the promise’ (Galatians 3:28-29).
passages.hard:
Does this law treat women fairly, if daughters inherit only when there are no sons?

The question is fair. The ruling works inside a system in which land passed through sons, and it does not overturn that system. Daughters inherit only where there is no son. Chapter 36 will add that these daughters must marry within their father's tribe. A reader who finds that troubling is noticing something real. The law assumes the social order of its time.

Two things can be said about what the chapter does within that order.

Some interpreters stress that God sides with five women who questioned a custom, says that they are right, and changes the law for all Israel because of them. They see here a principle that reaches beyond its setting: God's concern to protect people whom a system would leave out, and to give them standing.

Others stress that the law's chief purpose is to keep land within the clan and a father's name alive, and that it is not mainly about the standing of women.

Both things can be true at once, and these notes do not choose between them. What the story plainly shows is that women could bring a case before God's court in their own voice and be told that they spoke correctly.

Nothing in the chapter supports the idea that a daughter is worth less than a son. And it gives no ground for denying a woman today her property, her voice, or her standing before the law.
passages.asks: The sisters asked for a share in a land no one yet held, and God said they were right. Ask what just thing you have not asked for because custom told you it was not for you. And ask whose case you could carry to those who decide, if they cannot easily bring it themselves.

passages.happening:
God says to Moses, “Go up this mountain of the Abarim range and see the land that I have given the Israelites. After you have seen it, you too will be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was” (verses 12-13). The reason is recalled: what happened at the waters of Meribah (verse 14).

Moses answers with a request. “May the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation who will go out and come in before them, and who will lead them out and bring them in, so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
The second half of the chapter turns to Moses. The sentence given after he struck the rock is about to take effect. He will see the land from a mountain and die on this side of the river. The Abarim range is the line of heights on the eastern edge of the Jordan valley. Deuteronomy names the peak as Mount Nebo.

Look at what Moses says when he is told. Elsewhere he asked God to let him cross (Deuteronomy 3:23-25). Here he says nothing about himself at all. He does not argue, and he does not grieve aloud. His whole answer is about the people. Who will lead them?

He addresses God as ‘the God of the spirits of all flesh’, the one who knows every person from the inside. Only such a God can choose the right leader.

His picture of a leader is plain. He wants someone who will ‘go out and come in before them’. That is a phrase for leading in battle and in daily life. A leader of this kind goes at the front. He does not send others where he will not go.

And he gives the reason in a picture every Israelite knew: sheep without a shepherd. Sheep left alone scatter, go hungry and are taken by wild animals. Across the ancient Near East kings were called the shepherds of their people. Moses had spent forty years as a real shepherd in Midian before he led Israel. His last request for his people is that they will not be left without one.

The chapter began with daughters asking that their father's name should not be lost. It goes on to a father of the nation asking that his people should not be lost. Both requests are about what will go on after a death, and God grants both.
passages.later:
The prophets promised a shepherd to come: “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them” (Ezekiel 34:23).

Mark uses Moses' own words of Jesus: “When Jesus stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And He began to teach them many things” (Mark 6:34).

And Jesus says of himself, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (John 10:11).
passages.asks: Told that he was about to die, Moses asked nothing for himself and prayed for the people he would leave. Ask what you would pray if you knew your work was nearly over. And ask who will care for the people you now care for, and whether you have asked God to provide for them.

passages.happening:
God answers, “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the Spirit in him, and lay your hands on him” (verse 18). Moses is to stand him before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation and commission him in their sight. “Confer on him some of your authority, so that the whole congregation of Israel will obey him” (verse 20).

Joshua will stand before Eleazar, ‘who will seek counsel for him before the LORD by the judgment of the Urim’ (verse 21).

Moses does as he is told. He stands Joshua before the priest and the people, “and laid his hands on him and commissioned him, as the LORD had instructed through Moses” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
God's choice is no stranger. Joshua led Israel's fighting men against Amalek soon after the exodus (Exodus 17). He was Moses' assistant from his youth. He was one of the two scouts who trusted God at Kadesh. He has been forty years in the making.

The text gives one qualification above the rest: he is ‘a man with the Spirit in him’. The gesture of laying on hands does not give him that. It recognizes what God has already done and hands on the task in public.

The laying on of hands marked the passing of a role from one person to another. It was done before witnesses so that no one could dispute it afterward. Moses had seen what rivalry over leadership could do. This handing on is done in the open, in front of the priest and all the people.

Moses gives Joshua ‘some’ of his authority. Joshua will not be a second Moses. Moses spoke with God face to face. Joshua will ask for God's direction through the high priest and the Urim. The Urim, with the Thummim named elsewhere, was a means kept by the high priest for seeking God's decision on particular questions. How it worked is not known.

So the new leader is placed under a check from the start. He leads the people, but he does not decide alone. He stands before the priest and asks.

Moses does exactly as he is told. He gives the work away, in front of everyone, to the man who will finish what he was not allowed to finish.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy looks back on this day: “Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him” (Deuteronomy 34:9).

The church took up the same gesture for setting people apart to serve. Paul reminds Timothy of the gift given ‘at the laying on of the hands of the elders’ (1 Timothy 4:14).

Hebrews notes that Joshua, whose name in Greek is the name Jesus, could bring Israel into the land but not into its final rest: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day” (Hebrews 4:8).
passages.asks: Moses handed on his work in public, with both hands, to the man who would go where he could not. Ask whether you hold on to a task or a position that it is time to give to someone else. And ask whether you could do it gladly, and tell everyone that you had.
